---
id: ex-isoparametric-unit-disk-mesh
kind: example
title: "A ten-cell isoparametric mesh exactly covers the unit disk"
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: numerical-analysis-remaining-71-2026-10-17
dependency_level: 2
deps:
  - def-isoparametric-curved-cell-map
  - lem-isoparametric-pullback-and-surface-metric
  - thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions
  - def-countable-choice
proof_strategy: direct
provenance:
  statement: ai-altered
  proof: ai-altered
sources:
  references:
    - title: "Jean-Luc Guermond, MATH 661 Fall 2023, Part III, Chapter 8"
      url: https://people.tamu.edu/~guermond/M661_FALL_2023/chap08.pdf
    - title: "Gerald Dziuk and Charles M. Elliott, Finite element methods for surface PDEs, Acta Numerica 22 (2013)"
      url: https://wrap.warwick.ac.uk/id/eprint/53966/1/WRAP_Elliott_DziEll13a.pdf
verification:
  precheck: pass
---

## Example

Assume Countable Choice. Let $a=1/2$ and $g(t)=a\tan(\pi t/4)$. Map the reference square $[-1,1]^2$ to the central square $[-a,a]^2$ by $H(t,q)=(g(t),g(q))$ and split it into two triangles. For the top annular sector use $\theta(t)=\pi/2-\pi t/4$, $r(s,t)=(1-s)a/\sin\theta(t)+s$, and $F(t,s)=r(s,t)(\cos\theta(t),\sin\theta(t))$; split this rectangle into two triangles and rotate it for the other three sides. These ten mapped triangles have positive Jacobians, matching traces, and union equal to the closed unit disk.

## Geometry sketch

The central square and four annular sectors are shown with their shared radial rays. Dashed lines indicate the chosen splits of the mapped sector rectangles; their exact curved images are given by $F$ above and the rotations, so the sketch is topological and is not used in the coverage proof.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=2]
  \coordinate (O) at (0,0);
  \draw[thick] (O) circle (1);
  \draw[thick] (-0.5,-0.5) rectangle (0.5,0.5);
  \draw[blue,thick] (-0.5,-0.5)--(0.5,0.5);
  \foreach \a in {45,135,225,315} {\draw (O)--({cos(\a)},{sin(\a)});}
  \draw[dashed,red] (-0.5,0.5)--({cos(45)},{sin(45)});
  \draw[dashed,red] (0.5,0.5)--({cos(135)},{sin(135)});
  \draw[dashed,red] (0.5,-0.5)--({cos(225)},{sin(225)});
  \draw[dashed,red] (-0.5,-0.5)--({cos(315)},{sin(315)});
  \node at (0,0.68) {$2$ central cells};
  \node at (0,0.88) {$8$ sector cells};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; $a=1/2$, the central map $H$, the sector map $F$, and four rotations by multiples of $\pi/2$.

[F1] [[def-isoparametric-curved-cell-map]]: each cell map must have a positive Jacobian and neighboring mapped traces must agree.

[F2] [[lem-isoparametric-pullback-and-surface-metric]]: the metric and surface factors are determined by the Gram matrices of the map derivatives.

[F3] [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]]: under Countable Choice, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism changes variables with its positive Jacobian.

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed exactly for [F3] ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Verification

1.1 $g'(t)=a(\pi/4)\sec^2(\pi t/4)>0$, so $H$ maps $[-1,1]$ bijectively onto $[-a,a]^2$, since $g(-1)=-a$ and $g(1)=a$. Its Gram determinant gives the same volume factor by [F2]. On the top sector, $\theta'=-\pi/4$ and $r_s=1-a/\sin\theta\ge1-a\sqrt2>0$ because $\sin\theta\ge\sqrt2/2$. Polar-coordinate differentiation gives $\det DF=r r_s(-\theta')>0$; the Gram determinant satisfies $\sqrt{\det(DF^TDF)}=\det DF$. Rotations preserve these determinants. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 At $s=0$, $F(t,0)=(a\cot\theta(t),a)=(g(t),a)$, which is exactly the trace of $H$ on its top edge; at $s=1$, $r=1$, so the outer trace is the unit-circle arc from angle $3\pi/4$ to $\pi/4$. The two radial side traces match those of adjacent rotated sectors. Hence all ten pieces meet only along identical mapped edges. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For each angle $\theta\in[\pi/4,3\pi/4]$, the square boundary on that ray has radius $a/\sin\theta$ and the unit-circle boundary has radius $1$. The sector map covers exactly the radii between them. Four rotated angular ranges cover the annulus outside the central square, with shared corner rays only; $H$ covers the central square. Therefore the ten mapped triangles cover the unit disk without interior overlap. [given, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The central area is $4a^2=1$. By [F3], the sector area is the polar integral $\frac12\int_{\pi/4}^{3\pi/4}(1-a^2\csc^2\theta)d\theta$. Since $[-\cot\theta]_{\pi/4}^{3\pi/4}=2$, this equals $\pi/4-a^2=(\pi-1)/4$. Four rotated sectors have total area $\pi-1$, so the union area is $\pi$, consistent with the unit disk. [F3, A1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

id: lem-curved-boundary-lift-residual
kind: lemma
title: Geometry error bounds a pulled-back boundary-lift residual
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: numerical-analysis-remaining-71-2026-10-17
dependency_level: 2
deps:

  - def-measure
  - thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives

proof_strategy: direct

sources:

      url: https://people.tamu.edu/~guermond/M661_FALL_2025/chap27.pdf
    - title: Gerald Dziuk and Charles M. Elliott, Finite element methods for surface PDEs, Acta Numerica 22 (2013)
      url: https://wrap.warwick.ac.uk/id/eprint/53966/1/WRAP_Elliott_DziEll13a.pdf
verification:
  precheck: pass
---

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\widehat\Omega=(-1,1)^2$ be covered by a finite matching cell mesh, and let $\Phi,\Phi_h$ be continuous geometry maps whose cellwise $C^1$ derivatives satisfy $\|D\Phi\|_\infty+\|D\Phi_h\|_\infty\le M$, $e_0=\|\Phi-\Phi_h\|_\infty$, and $e_1=\|D\Phi-D\Phi_h\|_{L^\infty;op}$. Let $G$ be a scalar physical boundary lift on an open convex neighborhood containing both images and every segment joining corresponding image points, with $\|DG\|_\infty\le L_1$ and $\|D^2G\|_\infty\le L_2$. Define the piecewise pullback gradients by $\nabla_{pw}(G\circ\Phi)=D\Phi^T\nabla G(\Phi)$ and $\nabla_{pw}(G\circ\Phi_h)=D\Phi_h^T\nabla G(\Phi_h)$, and set
$$\ell_{\partial,h}(w)=\int_{\widehat\Omega}\big(\nabla_{pw}(G\circ\Phi)-\nabla_{pw}(G\circ\Phi_h)\big)\cdot\nabla w,\qquad w\in H^1_0(\widehat\Omega).$$
With the $H^1$ dual norm, $\|\ell_{\partial,h}\|_{(H^1_0)^*}\le 2(L_1e_1+ML_2e_0)$. Thus the geometry-induced boundary-lift contribution to the Strang load defect is $O(e_0+e_1)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; the reference square; continuous, cellwise $C^1$ maps with the stated derivative gap and upper bound; a $C^2$ lift $G$ on a convex neighborhood of both images; and $w\in H^1_0(\widehat\Omega)$.

[F1] [[def-curved-domain-geometry-approximation]]: $e_0$ and $e_1$ are the uniform value and derivative gaps between exact and approximate geometry maps.

[F2] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: $D(G\circ\Phi)=D\Phi^T(DG\circ\Phi)$ wherever the cell maps are differentiable.

[F3] [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]: $|\int f\cdot g|\le\|f\|_{L^2}\|g\|_{L^2}$.

[F4] Under Countable Choice, the Lebesgue measurable sets form a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set, and Lebesgue measure agrees there with elementary volume. For the half-open box $B=[-1,1)^2$, its elementary volume is $4$.
([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]],
[[thm-elementary-volume-is-well-defined]],
[[def-half-open-box]],
[[def-elementary-set-in-rn]])

[F5] A measure is nonnegative and finitely additive on disjoint measurable sets; consequently it is monotone on measurable sets, since $E\subseteq B$ gives $B=E\cup(B\setminus E)$.
([[def-measure]])

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed exactly for [F4] ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

1.1 Because each geometry map and its traces are continuous across every interior facet, $G\circ\Phi$ and $G\circ\Phi_h$ have matching traces there. For a compactly supported smooth test function, integration by parts cell by cell cancels the interior-facet terms; the outer boundary term vanishes because the test is compactly supported. Thus the displayed piecewise gradients are the weak gradients of the pulled-back lifts. On each cell, [F2] and the triangle inequality give $|\nabla_{pw}(G\circ\Phi)-\nabla_{pw}(G\circ\Phi_h)|\le L_1e_1+ML_2e_0,$ using the bound on $D^2G$ along the joining segment. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 For $n\ge2$ put $B_n=[-1+1/n,1-1/n)^2$. Each $B_n$ is an elementary half-open box, and $(-1,1)^2=\bigcup_{n\ge2}B_n$: one inclusion is immediate, and for any $x\in(-1,1)^2$ choose $n$ with $1/n<\min_i\{1+x_i,1-x_i\}$ for both coordinates. Thus [F4] makes $\widehat\Omega$ measurable. Since $\widehat\Omega\subset B=[-1,1)^2$, [F5] and [F4] give $|\widehat\Omega|\le\lambda_2(B)=4$. Step 1.1 therefore yields $\|\nabla_{pw}(G\circ\Phi)-\nabla_{pw}(G\circ\Phi_h)\|_{L^2(\widehat\Omega)}\le 2(L_1e_1+ML_2e_0).$ [F4, F5, A1, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F3] to the defining integral for $\ell_{\partial,h}(w)$ and use $\|\nabla w\|_{L^2}\le\|w\|_{H^1}$. Taking the supremum over unit $H^1_0$ tests proves the dual bound. [F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

disk_full_verification.review: g has positive bounded derivative on a neighborhood of the closed interval; its coordinate product maps the square bijectively to the central square with determinant gprime(t)gprime(q)>0. On the sector, angle is strictly monotone and radius strictly increases in s, with rs>=1-sqrt(2)/2>0 and positive r. Thus det DF=-r rs theta_prime>0. The polar inverse determines t from angle and s from radius, and extends through the closed rectangle on a slightly larger neighborhood because y>0, angle length is below a full turn and rs stays positive. Compactness supplies finite derivative/inverse bounds on the ten closed triangles.

At the inner sector side, a cot(theta)=a tan(pi t/4)=g(t), agreeing exactly with H on the top edge. At s=1 the map is the quarter-circle arc. Along corner rays adjacent rotated sectors have identical radial interpolation; affine edge orientation reversal accounts for the shared parameter direction. Both diagonal splits are restrictions of one map, so their own diagonals match.

Each top angle from pi/4 to3pi/4 has a unique square-exit radius a/sin(theta) strictly below1. Radial interpolation covers exactly that segment. Four rotated angle sectors share only corner rays and cover all points outside the central square up to radius1. H covers the square; the two+eight triangle interiors are disjoint. Domain boundary points are included, giving the closed disk.

Central area4a^2=1. Polar sector integral is one half of pi/2 minus one half times a^2 times the csc-squared integral2, giving pi/4-a^2=(pi-1)/4. Four sectors plus center yield pi; positive Jacobians license the change of variables.

lift_full_proof.review: On each closed triangle the composite lift is C1. Integration by parts against a compactly supported smooth test is licensed on each actual affine triangle. Opposing facet normals and identical composite traces cancel every interior term; the outer term vanishes. Bounded finite piecewise derivatives give the true global weak gradients. Splitting the gradient difference as (DPhi-DPhih)^T gradG(Phi)+DPhih^T(gradG(Phi)-gradG(Phih)) bounds it by L1e1+ML2e0, since DPhih norm is at most the supplied sum M and the Hessian bound is valid along every connecting segment.

For n>=2 the boxes(-1+1/n,1-1/n]^2 are legitimate elementary boxes and increase to the open square. Every point is in some box by a positive minimum distance to all four boundaries. Measurable sigma closure gives the square; containment in(-1,1]^2 and monotonicity give measure<=4. The pointwise gradient bound therefore has L2 norm at most2 times its constant.

Each weak test gradient is L2 and the gradient-gap field is bounded on a finite-measure square, hence L2. Holder makes the residual integral finite and bounds it by the gap norm times the H1 norm of the test. Taking the unit-sphere supremum gives the stated dual norm.

actual_review.boundary_cases: Disk endpoints t=+-1 and s=0,1 are included with positive determinant; no collapsed sector occurs because a=1/2<1/sqrt2. The nonempty reference square and nondegenerate triangles exclude empty/collapsed-domain issues. No critical limiting Jacobian is claimed.
